decisions.text: Secrets sit beside the levels, not on the ladder: secrets is a config key orthogonal to the level, as packs is, measured by its own secrets.* rows whatever the level reads; Level 2's requirement list claims those rows when Level 2 opens. No charter amendment.

The age ciphertext is tracked: secrets/<target>.env.age and secrets/recipients.txt are committed, so a clone plus the identity is a working machine. The identity, passphrase-protected and outside the repo, is the only secret.
Proof is required to read PASS: a target without a proof is WARN in doctor and unproved on the banner (rule 2: a chosen state, with the reason).

Plan approved with five P2 amendments (dispositions 42 to 46) and the two answers to §12 (dispositions 47, 48); dispositions 1 to 41, the residue in §11 and the five-session split accepted as planned.

Rule 3: run splits its argv at the first -- before parseArgv; everything after it is the child's verbatim, flags included; no -- or nothing after it is the usage, exit 2. A target name is ^[a-z][a-z0-9-]*$, a secret name ^[A-Z][A-Z0-9_]*$, both validated by the config.

Rules 3 and 7: a proof names the names it covers, never infers them by value shape. { kind: supabase, ref, names? } defaults names to those of SUPABASE_URL and DB_URL the target declares (invalid when neither); { kind: host, host, names } requires names. A covered name must be declared; a covered value that does not satisfy the kind is a mismatch, never skipped; a proof covering zero names is invalid.

Rule 2: a target without proof is secrets.targets WARN and unproved on the banner; a declared proof that fails refuses the run with the kind's reason (the name, the expected identifier, the anchor that failed; a found ref only when the value parsed as a *.supabase.co URL; never a value, host or password).

Rule 1 governs hooks; run is the user's own command and refusing is the product: a missing tool, wrong platform, missing name, a literal in a template, a failed proof, a malformed resolved line, a value on the child's command line each print one line naming the fix, exit 125 (disposition 47), nothing spawned. The hooks are unchanged.

Rule 3: redaction costs the child its output terminal, said not weakened: stdin inherited, stdout and stderr piped through the redactor (no TTY on them: no colour unless forced, no pager), the banner says so once. Redacted: every injected value, its encodeURIComponent form, and for a URL-shaped value a password of 8+ characters alone, decoded and encoded, each replaced by <NAME>. The guide says these are the forms covered.

Rules 5 and 7: secrets/ is a fixed directory at the config root; the ciphertext is armored (age -a), text, through the pre-commit scan like any file. The identity lives at $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/cookwright/identity.age (~/.config when unset) or COOKWRIGHT_AGE_IDENTITY, never under the work tree judged by realpath: secrets init refuses such a path and doctor FAILs it.

Rule 3: doctor never prompts. 1password: the template is parsed. keychain: items found by attributes (find-generic-password -s -a, no -w), present by name; whether that can raise the unlock dialog on a locked keychain is measured in QA and the row reads not measured if it can. age: the three files exist and are tracked; the identity header (age-encryption.org/v1) decides passphrase-protected else WARN naming the upgrade; the note never interpolates the line; nothing is decrypted.
Rule 9: no dependency. Echo-off input is setRawMode on a terminal stdin; no pseudo-terminal for the child.

Rule 4: backends behind one interface in src/lib/secrets/backends/, reaching their tools only through two new probes: capture (synchronous runBounded with input; budget-bounded inside doctor, 120 s cap outside, uncapped when the call prompts on a terminal) and spawnChild (asynchronous spawn, never shell: true). The engine is tested with a fake backend and fake probes; each tool once for real.

Rule 7, deviating from the kickoff's keychain sentence: security add-generic-password takes the value only as an argument or through its own prompt, so secrets set on keychain runs it with -w last and the terminal inherited; the value never reaches cookwright. For age, secrets set reads from a terminal prompt with echo off, or one line from stdin with --stdin (a visible flag); without either it refuses. Never from an argument. secrets init asks for consent, pipes the key through age -p -o <identity> (binary), captures age's stderr and refuses on an autogenerated passphrase; --no-passphrase writes the key as generated, mode 600, the WARN state.

Rule 6: E-015 closes here. secrets.carriers reads .envrc tracked or at the root, any declared or ambient name present in doctor's own environment, and a line setting such a name in ~/.zshenv, ~/.zshrc, ~/.zprofile, ~/.bashrc, ~/.bash_profile, ~/.profile (names and file names only; comments skipped). It guards repo.config and repo.workTree itself. With no secrets key it still checks .envrc.

Rule 3: the keychain backend's real test uses a throwaway keychain (create, unlock, no auto-lock, in a scratch dir, deleted in afterAll, a vitest timeout) through an optional keychain argument the product never passes; items are added by the test with -w <value> <keychain> (test-only); resolve and inspect exercised; set's prompted path is the developer's QA. npm test never touches a login keychain.

Rule 3: run's exit is the child's status; 128 + signal number on a signal; 127 when the command could not be spawned; 125 for a refusal before spawn. cookwright ignores SIGINT and SIGTERM while the child runs, waits for it, sets process.exitCode and lets the loop drain; after exit the pipes drain for at most 200 ms then end(). The banner goes to stderr. The child's cwd is process.cwd().

Rules 2 and 3: the child's environment is the inherited one with every declared name of every target, every ambient name, and any variable whose value equals a resolved value removed, then the target's values added; each removed name is on the banner as dropped from the environment. cookwright's own process.env is left as inherited; values live in one Map until spawn.

Rule 3: a 1Password template line is NAME=op://<vault>/<item>/[<section>/]<field> with each segment [A-Za-z0-9 ._-]+ (no $, { or }), a blank line, or a # comment that does not look like NAME=; any other line is a literal: doctor FAILs and run refuses naming the line number, never the line. op inject -f -i <tpl> runs with the scrubbed environment. Output parsed as NAME=value at the first =, no trimming; an empty value is missing; a malformed line is refused by number.
Rule 5: the 3→4 migration changes nothing but the version (outcome secretsNone); freshConfig writes no secrets key.
Rule 3: secrets.backend reads PASS no backend (Level 2 off) and secrets.targets PASS no targets declared when secrets is absent, measured facts, so the three rows are static (22 rows on this repo).

Rules 3 and 4: proof kinds are a registry: core host plus proofs from each declared pack's manifest (data and pure functions importing nothing). The config validates proof.kind against host and the declared packs' kinds, one home, as it validates pack rules; an unknown kind is an invalid config naming the pack that has it.

Rule 3: the supabase kind is the origin's anchored check with the kickoff's <role>.<ref>: project URL https://<ref>.supabase.co; database URL names the ref as the pooler username ^[a-z_][a-z0-9_]*\.<ref>$ on a host ending in .pooler.supabase.com, or as the direct host db.<ref>.supabase.co; when both appear they must agree; userinfo split at the last @, never by new URL. The host kind compares new URL(value).host with the declared host canonicalised the same way. A ref is ^[a-z]{20}$.

Rule 7: nothing in the stage prints a value: tests assert on length or sha256; the fixture's synthetic values are asserted by length through the child; the closeout records the 1Password run's banner only.
Rule 7: before spawning, run checks every argument after -- for a needle as a substring (the value and its encoded form); a match refuses naming the name and the argument's position.

Rule 7: the argv check's needles are the resolved values and the inherited values of every declared and ambient name (the ones childEnv drops), so -- psql "$DB_URL" after a stale prod export is refused for the dev run; an argument of the shape <scheme>://<user>:<password>@ is refused regardless, loopback hosts excepted (disposition 43).

Rule 7: secrets set and secrets init's append refuse when secrets/recipients.txt is untracked or differs from HEAD; every line is age1[a-z0-9]{58} or a comment, an AGE-SECRET-KEY- line refused; the recipient count and each key's last eight characters are printed; secrets.targets WARNs when the file differs from HEAD; init on a fresh repo creates the file and says to commit it before the first set.
Rule 2: the identity is written binary (age -p -o, no -a) so the header check holds for an identity made the recommended way; only the ciphertext in the repo is armored.

Rule 3: the streaming redactor holds back only a tail that is a prefix of some needle, writes everything else at once (a prompt shows immediately, no timer), and releases a held tail only on more input, a newline that breaks the prefix, or end().

Rule 7: keychain items are per repo: service cookwright/<id>/<target> with id = secrets.id when set else the config root's basename; the banner, secrets set and the doctor row print the service; the default search list is used (residue §11); the guide names secrets.id for a renamed directory.

Rule 3: the child's own command line is the child's, and the guide says so beside the environment-block residual; the guide shows a wrapper that reads the environment and hands libpq a password-less URL with PGPASSWORD; PG* derivation inside run is noted on E-001.
Rule 3: doctor's age row measures files, not names; the fixture's assertions say so (superseded in wording by disposition 45).

Rule 3: a pack manifest may declare ambient names its tools read on their own (supabase: SUPABASE_DB_URL, SUPABASE_ACCESS_TOKEN, PGPASSWORD, PGPASSFILE, PGSERVICE, PGSERVICEFILE); run drops and names them; secrets.carriers names them when present; the registry test accepts the key.
Rule 3: the template grammar forbids $ and braces (op inject expands them from the environment) and op inject runs with -f and the scrubbed environment.

A second error class, Refused, printed as run: <reason> (or secrets: <reason>) with exit 125; Refusal stays usage and config problems, exit 2, through the shared refuse().

age -d with a passphrase-protected identity and no terminal is refused before spawning; on a terminal the call is uncapped.
On Windows the engine never uses a shell, the age row SKIPs the identity's permissions with the reason, the keychain backend SKIPs; nothing else is claimed (B-008 stands).

Rules 2 and 3: an existing app may ignore secrets/ already. secrets init and doctor's secrets.targets ask git (probes.ignored) whether secrets/, secrets/recipients.txt and each target's file are ignored; ignored reads FAIL naming the .gitignore line to remove, and init writes nothing. The configurable directory stays backlog.

Rule 3: the URL-with-password argv refusal exempts loopback hosts (localhost, 127.0.0.0/8, ::1, host.docker.internal): the local Supabase stack with its public password has no finding; those hosts still get the needle check.

Rule 2: an empty targets object is a valid config. With a backend set and no target, secrets.targets reads WARN no targets declared; add one (the secrets guide), never an invalid config that SKIPs every config row; a developer mid-setup is a chosen state.

Rule 3 (the B-013 lesson): the age line of secrets.targets claims only what it tests: ciphertext and recipients present and tracked reads PASS dev: ciphertext and recipients tracked, the names not mentioned; the guide says a missing name surfaces at run. not measured never appears on a PASS line; where a backend cannot measure the thing a row names, the row is SKIP with the reason; secrets.backend for 1password reads PASS op on PATH.

Rule 6: one identity per developer, said in the guide and by secrets init; a second machine copies the identity and does not run init; init on a repo whose recipients.txt already holds a key says so and asks before appending; a second recipient needs every ciphertext re-encrypted, which nothing in this stage does: secrets rekey goes to the backlog and the guide names the limit.

Rule 3: pre-spawn refusals exit 125, so a wrapper, the gate included, tells cookwright refused from the child returned 1; 127 for ENOENT and 128+signal follow the shell's codes; the gate's exit 11 is the precedent. The fixture's refusal assertions read 125.

Rule 7: secrets set on keychain lets security prompt for the value with -w last and the terminal inherited; the kickoff's wording would have put the value on security's command line; the deviation is recorded.

The keychain service defaults to the config root's basename, so renaming the directory loses the items; the guide names secrets.id for that. secrets.carriers flags a line setting NAME in an rc file even when it holds no value (NAME=$(op read …)): names only, a WARN, the note saying a line setting NAME.

The child additionally loses each backend's control names (1password: OP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_TOKEN, OP_CONNECT_HOST, OP_CONNECT_TOKEN, every OP_SESSION_*; age: COOKWRIGHT_AGE_IDENTITY), named on the banner as dropped. decisions.source: plan-review round 1, findings 2 and 22 (P1, P2 confirmed), plan §2 disposition 51

On POSIX the identity must be mode 0600 and its directory 0700: init writes them so, doctor FAILs a group- or world-readable identity naming chmod 600; Windows per disposition 41. Tested with a symlinked config dir into a second scratch repo and a 0644 identity.

decisions.text: Rule 3: resolved output is parsed against the expected set. 1password: exactly one line per template reference, the same names in the same order, no other line; age: every line NAME=value with each declared name at most once and no undeclared name (secrets set refuses an undeclared name); a NUL, a duplicate, an unknown or a missing declared name refuses naming the name or the line number only; an empty value is missing; a multi-line field is refused as an extra line. Adversarial tests: a continuation line shaped LD_PRELOAD=x, a duplicate, an unknown name, a NUL.

decisions.text: Rule 3: a backend declares its tools per operation (age: resolve needs age, init needs age and age-keygen); secrets.backend names the missing one; secrets.targets SKIPs with the backend row's reason whenever that row is SKIP or FAIL, never calling inspect. decisions.source: plan-review round 1, findings 10, 17 and 26 (P2, P1, P3), plan §2 disposition 59
decisions.text: Rule 3: the redactor works on bytes: needles are Buffers (raw and encoded forms) matched with Buffer.indexOf, the prefix hold-back on bytes, bytes passed unchanged when nothing matches, so a binary stream (pg_dump -Fc, tar, gzip) comes through byte-identical. It is a Transform piped with normal backpressure, and run exits only after both pipes have closed and the child has exited: no 200 ms drain. A daemonising grandchild keeps run alive until it closes its output, as a shell pipeline would; the guide says to redirect such output inside the command. Tests: random binary and a pg_dump-shaped header byte-identical; invalid UTF-8 untouched; a slow consumer with a large output; a grandchild holding the pipe for a second.

decisions.source: plan-review round 1, finding 16 (P1 confirmed), plan §2 disposition 60, PROVISIONAL pending the developer
decisions.text: Rule 7: security's prompt truncates at 128 characters silently (measured: getpass(3), _PASSWORD_LEN), which a service-role JWT and most pooler URLs exceed, so decision 48's mechanism cannot stand. Provisionally: secrets set on keychain reads the value through cookwright's own echo-off prompt (or --stdin), writes it through security -i (the interactive mode reading the add-generic-password line from stdin, so the value is on no command line), s3 measures security -i's quoting and limits (220 characters, spaces, quotes, non-ASCII) before building on it, and after every set reads the item back with -w and compares sha256 with the input, refusing otherwise. If security -i fails the measurement, the keychain set refuses values the OS cannot store faithfully and the limit goes to the guide and the developer. The ruling is the developer's (contradicts decision 48 on a measurement).
